rows.intervention: short contact cryotherapy, single freeze of 3-5 s per macule, once a month until repigmentation, maximum 3 applications
rows.comparator: 88% phenol applied to 5 other IGH macules of the same patient
rows.arm_result: 75/125 (60%) macules excellent (>75% improvement); 20/125 (16%) good (51-75%); [30/125 (24%)] minimal or no response combined (not reported separately); P < 0.05 vs phenol (comparison not specified)
rows.texture_or_scar: not in abstract as counts; abstract states persistent scabbing and ulceration were more common with 88% phenol than with cryotherapy
rows.uncertainty: Abstract only. No untreated control macules are reported, although every patient had more than 10 macules, so spontaneous change cannot be separated from treatment effect. Within-patient comparison: each patient contributes 5 macules to each arm, and the abstract does not say how macules were allocated, who graded them, whether grading was blinded, or whether the P < 0.05 test accounted for clustering within patients; the test's comparison (which grade or grades) is not stated. 125 = [25 completers x 5 macules], so results cover completers only; the [25] macules per arm from the [5] patients who dropped out are not analysed. The grading scale has gaps and overlaps in the abstract: Grade 1 is '<25%' and Grade 2 '26%-50%', so 25% falls in no grade, and there is no separate grade for no change. Minimal and no-response counts are not given separately. The schedule sentence is ambiguous: 'single cryotherapy for 3-5 s was applied for another 5 IGH macules once in a month till the repigmentation for maximum of 3 applications' can be read as applying the monthly, up-to-3 schedule to cryotherapy only or to both arms; the number of applications each macule received is not reported, so time from each macule's final treatment cannot be derived. Results are given only 'At the end of the treatment period', with no visit after treatment ended, so durability is not measured. The conclusion calls cryotherapy 'more efficacious and safe', but side effects are described only qualitatively (no counts). Duplicate-cohort check: the abstract gives no study site, recruitment dates or ethics approval, so overlap with other cohorts cannot be settled from this text. The authors' department (Mandya Institute of Medical Sciences) and three author names (Rajegowda, Kalegowda/Deepadarshan, Madegowda/Shashikumar) are shared with deepadarshan2023 in the ledger, whose own source (papers/excerpts/deepadarshan2023.txt, not this text) reports a different treatment (308 nm excimer laser) run from August 2022 to January 2023, after this article's 2021 publication [so the two are probably not the same cohort, although individual patients could recur; this abstract gives no dates or patient details to check]. The earlier lead note's 'near-identical title' article in J Pak Assoc Dermatol was not identified in this source text.

quotes.quote: A total of 30 patients with more than 10 IGH macules were selected.
A total of 25 patients completed the study.
For each enrolled patient, 88% phenol was applied to 5 IGH macules and single cryotherapy for 3–5 s was applied for another 5 IGH macules
once in a month till the repigmentation for maximum of 3 applications. Patients were assessed monthly for 3 months for the side effects and improvement in pigmentation.

The degree of improvement in pigmentation was assessed using a grading system, <25% - no response (Grade-1), 26%–50% - minimal (Grade-2), 51%–75% - good (Grade-3), and >75% - excellent response (Grade-4).
Side effects such as persistent scabbing, ulceration were more common with 88% phenol application compared to cryotherapy.
Department of Dermatology, Venereology and Leprosy, Mandya Institute of Medical Sciences, Mandya, Karnataka, India
